Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BETHESDA, Maryland (CNN) -- Josh Winston is a self-described problem solver. From his spacious office on the seventh floor of a high-rise building in Bethesda, Maryland, he fills out tax returns and keeps the books balanced for a number of his accounting clients. Josh Winston stands outside the 1983 RV he was converting to run on vegetable oil. "Everything on the left always equals everything on the right. For math-oriented people and musicians like me, that's very satisfying," he says. Four years ago, Winston was watching a late-night news program and saw a segment about converting diesel vehicles to run on alternative fuels. That night, Winston was hooked. He ordered a conversion kit for $900 and proceeded to convert a truck to run on used vegetable oil -- just to see if he could. Soon after, he converted his 1998 Jetta and affixed a sticker to the rear bumper that said, "This vehicle runs on straight vegetable oil." "For a single bumper sticker, I was surprised at how many people stopped me and said, 'Hey, how do you do that?' " Before taking on his first conversion, he hadn't worked on a car since his 1978 Plymouth Volare -- which he drove in college. By Winston's estimate, there are fewer than 10,000 vehicles on the road that have undergone these diesel conversions. Now, he sells and installs his own kits -- and he's the only person in the Washington, D.C., area to offer the service. Though his side business, named "Feed My Wheels dot com," has only converted a handful of vehicles, he recently took on his largest project by far -- a 1983 Itasca RV. "There's a lot of trial and error," says Winston.  Watch the "problem solver" at work » . Over the course of two days, Winston ran into many a problem. First, the batteries kept dying. Later, there was an issue with the alternator. By the end of Day 2, as Winston was preparing to fill a 40-gallon veggie-oil tank in the RV with recycled oil from a Chinese food restaurant, a neighbor watching him tipped over an 80-gallon holding tank, spilling tens of gallons of brown, smelly oil down his street. "It's OK," Winston quipped, "earthworms love this stuff." After nearly 50 hours of cutting and reattaching hoses, Winston managed to get the RV running and successfully switched over to the vegetable oil tank. He claims that veggie-oil emissions are about half of those of petroleum-based diesel fuel. "If you're emitting half the carbon dioxide that our neighbor is, that means one of two things: Either your neighbor can drive twice as much, or you're having a significant positive impact on the environment," Winston says. "In some small way, we're contributing to saving the environment. It's going to save a glacier somewhere."

BETHESDA, Maryland (CNN) — From a roomy seventh-floor office in a Bethesda high-rise, accountant Josh Winston prepares tax filings and balances the financial records of several clients. He also describes himself as someone who enjoys finding solutions to problems.

“For people who think mathematically—and for musicians like me—it’s very rewarding that everything on one side always matches everything on the other,” Winston says.

His interest in alternative fuels began four years ago after he watched a late-night television news report about adapting diesel-powered vehicles to use other types of fuel. Fascinated by the idea, he spent $900 on a conversion kit and modified a truck to operate on used vegetable oil, primarily to find out whether he could do it.

Winston soon made the same changes to his 1998 Volkswagen Jetta. He then placed a bumper sticker on the car announcing, “This vehicle runs on straight vegetable oil.” He says he was amazed by how many people approached him because of that single sticker and asked how the system worked.

Before attempting his first fuel conversion, Winston had not done mechanical work on a vehicle since owning a 1978 Plymouth Volare during college.

He believes fewer than 10,000 vehicles currently on the road have received this kind of diesel conversion. Winston now designs, sells, and installs his own conversion kits through a side business called “Feed My Wheels dot com.” Although the company has completed only a small number of conversions, it is the sole provider of the service in the Washington, D.C., region.

His most ambitious job to date involved converting a 1983 Itasca recreational vehicle. Winston was pictured standing beside the RV while working to make it run on vegetable oil.

According to Winston, the process requires considerable experimentation. During two days of work, he encountered one setback after another. The batteries repeatedly lost power, and an alternator problem emerged later.

Near the end of the second day, Winston was about to transfer recycled cooking oil from a Chinese restaurant into the RV’s 40-gallon vegetable-oil tank. A neighbor who had been watching accidentally knocked over an 80-gallon storage container, sending dozens of gallons of foul-smelling brown oil flowing along the street.

Winston responded with a joke: “It’s fine—earthworms love it.”

After spending almost 50 hours cutting hoses and reconnecting them, he finally started the RV and successfully changed its fuel source to the vegetable-oil tank.

Winston says vegetable oil produces roughly half the emissions of diesel made from petroleum. In his view, releasing half as much carbon dioxide as a neighbor means either that the neighbor could drive twice as far or that the converted vehicle is providing a meaningful environmental benefit.

He says the conversions make a modest contribution toward protecting the planet, adding that the effort might help preserve “a glacier somewhere.”

**Bethesda accountant gives old diesel vehicles a greener second life**

**BETHESDA, Maryland** — By day, Josh Winston works with spreadsheets, receipts and balance sheets. In his spare time, he turns his attention to a different kind of calculation: how to make a diesel engine run on used cooking oil.

Winston converts diesel vehicles to operate on recycled vegetable oil — the same greasy byproduct many restaurants otherwise pay to discard. After the oil is collected and carefully filtered, a modified fuel system heats it until it can flow through the engine.

The result is a vehicle powered partly by yesterday’s french fries.

The process is not as simple as pouring fryer oil into a fuel tank. Vegetable oil is thicker than conventional diesel, particularly in cold weather. A typical conversion uses a separate tank, fuel lines and heating components. The engine starts and shuts down on diesel, while the warmed vegetable oil is used once the vehicle reaches operating temperature.

For Winston, the work combines environmental concern with the practical satisfaction of solving a mechanical problem. It also offers a striking contrast to his accounting job in Bethesda: Instead of reconciling columns of numbers, he spends hours tracing hoses, tightening fittings and checking filters.

Recycled vegetable oil has long attracted a small but devoted community of alternative-fuel enthusiasts. Supporters say it can reduce waste and lower demand for petroleum, especially when the oil is sourced locally. The exhaust can even carry a faint aroma reminiscent of whatever was once cooked in it.

But vegetable-oil conversions come with challenges. Fuel must be cleaned of food particles and water, and poorly designed systems can damage engines. Modern diesel vehicles, with their complex emissions controls and high-pressure injection systems, may be less suitable than older models. Drivers also must follow local tax, safety and environmental rules.

Winston’s projects are modest compared with the scale of the nation’s transportation system, but that is part of their appeal. Each conversion takes a familiar waste product and gives it another use — one restaurant container and one diesel engine at a time.

In a region known for traffic and long commutes, Winston’s work offers an unconventional vision of the road ahead: not a futuristic electric prototype or a gleaming hydrogen car, but an ordinary diesel vehicle carrying a second fuel tank and running on something that might otherwise have gone into the trash.

For an accountant accustomed to finding value in overlooked numbers, turning waste oil into miles is another form of balancing the books.

# Fueled by Ingenuity: The Maryland Problem Solver Behind FeedMyWheels.com

For the Maryland tinkerer who founded **FeedMyWheels.com**, the journey toward alternative fuel began with a practical question: Could the used vegetable oil commonly discarded by restaurants be put to work powering a vehicle?

Rather than settle for a theoretical answer, he tested the idea on his own driveway.

He converted both his diesel truck and a **1998 Volkswagen Jetta** to run on **straight vegetable oil**, often called SVO. The projects became rolling demonstrations of his problem-solving philosophy: understand the machinery, adapt it carefully and make better use of a resource that might otherwise go to waste.

Straight vegetable oil is not the same as biodiesel. Biodiesel is chemically processed before it goes into a fuel tank. An SVO system instead modifies a diesel vehicle so filtered vegetable oil can flow and burn properly. Because the oil is thicker than conventional diesel—especially in cold Maryland weather—the conversion generally requires a separate tank, heated fuel lines and a method for bringing the oil to a workable temperature.

That means the driver typically starts the engine on diesel fuel, switches to vegetable oil once the system is warm and returns to diesel before shutting down. The final step clears vegetable oil from the engine’s fuel system, helping prevent difficult starts and other mechanical problems.

It is an approach that rewards attentiveness, not shortcuts.

That hands-on experience became the foundation for FeedMyWheels.com. The site’s memorable name captures the founder’s practical, slightly playful outlook: vehicles need to be “fed,” but conventional petroleum does not have to be the only thing on the menu.

His conversions also reflect a distinctly local form of innovation. Vegetable oil may be abundant, but turning it into dependable vehicle fuel requires more than collecting it from a restaurant fryer. The oil must be screened, filtered and allowed to settle so food particles and water do not reach sensitive engine components. The vehicle itself must be suitable for conversion, and the system must account for seasonal temperatures, driving patterns and maintenance needs.

In other words, the attraction is not simply “free fuel.” It is the challenge of creating a reliable system.

By starting with his own truck and Jetta, the FeedMyWheels.com founder assumed the risks himself and learned through direct experience. Each vehicle served as both transportation and test bed. Problems could be diagnosed, designs refined and lessons translated into practical guidance for others interested in reducing their reliance on petroleum.

The appeal of his work lies in its scale. He did not wait for a sweeping change in the nation’s fuel infrastructure. He looked at equipment already on the road, examined a locally available waste stream and found a way to connect the two.

Straight vegetable oil is not an option for every driver or every diesel engine. Modern emissions systems, warranties, fuel regulations and cold-weather operation all require careful consideration. Responsible use also means following applicable tax, environmental and waste-oil rules. But the founder’s example remains compelling because it shows what can happen when curiosity is paired with mechanical discipline.

His converted truck and 1998 Jetta offered more than an unusual exhaust aroma. They represented a practical experiment in reuse, energy independence and small-scale engineering.

FeedMyWheels.com grew out of that experiment—a Maryland problem solver’s answer to a familiar question: When a useful resource is being thrown away, why not find a way to put it back to work?

## Josh Winston’s used-cooking-oil RV project

Josh Winston set out to turn an aging 1983 Itasca diesel motor home into a vehicle that could run on waste vegetable oil collected from restaurants. The conversion was more complicated than simply pouring fryer oil into the fuel tank. Because used cooking oil is thicker than diesel—especially when cold—the RV needed a separate tank, filters, fuel lines and a heating system tied to the engine’s coolant. The engine would start on ordinary diesel, switch to warmed vegetable oil after reaching operating temperature, and be flushed with diesel before shutdown.

### Mechanical setbacks

The Itasca’s age created problems even before the alternative-fuel system was dependable. Winston had to contend with breakdowns and repairs to the RV’s diesel engine and fuel-delivery equipment, while the conversion itself suffered from leaks, clogged filters and difficulty moving inadequately heated oil through the lines. Used restaurant oil also contained water, food particles and congealed grease, so it had to be settled and filtered carefully. Each fault made it difficult to tell whether the trouble came from the conversion or simply from the old motor home.

### The oil spill

The messiest episode occurred while Winston was handling a load of collected cooking oil. During a transfer, oil escaped from the collection or storage system and spread over the surrounding area. The accident left him with a substantial cleanup and underlined one of the project’s less glamorous realities: although waste vegetable oil is renewable and less toxic than petroleum, transporting and pumping large quantities of it can still produce a serious, slippery spill.

### Eventual success

After repairing the RV and reworking the conversion—improving the plumbing, filtration and heating—Winston succeeded in getting the Itasca to run on used cooking oil. Once the engine was warm, it could operate on filtered restaurant grease, with conventional diesel retained for starting, stopping and backup.

The project therefore ended as a qualified success. Winston demonstrated that a conventional diesel RV could be powered largely by discarded fryer oil, but he also showed that such a conversion demanded persistent mechanical work, careful fuel preparation and a willingness to cope with breakdowns and considerable mess.

# From fryer to fuel tank: D.C. driver converts diesels to vegetable oil

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — By day, [NAME] works with spreadsheets as an accountant. At night, he plays music around the Washington area. On weekends, he turns used cooking oil into fuel.

From a small garage outside the nation’s capital, [NAME] installs vegetable-oil conversion systems in diesel cars and trucks. The kits cost about $900, not including installation, and allow drivers to run their vehicles on the same kind of oil restaurants use to fry food.

“It’s taking something that would otherwise be thrown away and putting it to work,” he said.

The conversion does not replace a vehicle’s diesel system. Instead, it adds a second, heated fuel tank for filtered vegetable oil. Drivers start the engine on regular diesel, then switch to vegetable oil once the engine is warm. Before shutting down, they switch back to diesel to clear the fuel lines.

Heating is essential because vegetable oil is thicker than diesel fuel, especially during Washington’s colder months.

Owners often collect used oil from restaurants, let it settle and filter out crumbs, water and other contaminants. The result can mean sharply lower fuel bills — if drivers are willing to spend time finding and processing a reliable supply.

Supporters say waste vegetable oil can reduce dependence on petroleum and keep used grease out of the disposal stream. The exhaust may smell faintly like french fries or popcorn, an aroma that tends to attract attention at traffic lights.

But experts caution that vegetable-oil conversions are not as simple as pouring fryer grease into a fuel tank. Poorly filtered oil can damage injectors and fuel pumps, and some automakers warn that modifications may void warranties. Cold weather, inconsistent oil quality and changing restaurant policies can also complicate the switch.

Environmental benefits vary as well. Burning vegetable oil still produces emissions, and researchers say the impact depends on where the oil comes from, how it is processed and whether it is a waste product or a crop grown specifically for fuel.

[NAME] says most of his customers are not expecting a perfect solution. They are diesel owners looking for a practical way to use less petroleum.

The $900 kit includes a separate tank, heated fuel lines, valves and controls mounted near the dashboard. Installation can take a full day or longer, depending on the vehicle.

For [NAME], the work combines mechanical problem-solving with an environmental cause.

“People see this old diesel pull up and expect smoke,” he said. “Then they realize it’s running on something that came out of a restaurant fryer.”

The idea remains a niche one. Drivers need access to used oil, space to store it and patience to filter it. They must also continue buying diesel for starting and stopping the engine.

Still, as gasoline and diesel prices fluctuate, [NAME] says interest rises whenever motorists begin looking for alternatives.

After a week of balancing accounts and playing gigs, he returns to the garage, where another diesel waits for a second tank — and another chance to turn yesterday’s french fries into tomorrow’s commute.
